analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health plan sold alongside private plans on the ACA marketplaces.
analysis.headline: The Medicare-X public option, introduced by 10 Senate Democrats in June 2024, never received a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a low-cost public health insurance plan run by the Department of Health and Human Services and sold on the ACA marketplaces, starting in areas with little insurer competition or provider shortages and reaching the whole country by 2029. It would pay doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates (up to 50% more in rural areas), require Medicare and Medicaid providers to join the plan, remove the income cap on ACA premium subsidies, fix the "family glitch," and fund antitrust enforcement against health care consolidation. It never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own or small-business health insurance — especially in counties with only one insurer, rural areas, or other high-cost markets — would get a government-run option that could undercut private premiums. Families earning above 400% of the poverty line, who currently get no ACA subsidies no matter how high premiums climb, would become eligible, and family members priced out of employer coverage would qualify for help. Medicare beneficiaries would gain from expanded drug price negotiation. Taxpayers would gain from $150 million in new antitrust funding aimed at hospital and insurer consolidation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying individual or small-group insurance

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare-based public plan sold on the ACA exchanges, starting where insurance competition is thinnest — areas with one or zero insurers, provider shortages, and rural regions — and available nationwide by plan year 2029.

Caps premiums only at the plan's actual cost with no profit margin, gives it free $2 billion in startup capital, and lets it pay providers at Medicare rates (up to 50% higher in rural areas), giving it a structural price advantage over private plans.

Removes the 400%-of-poverty income cap on ACA premium tax credits and lowers the share of income families must pay at every income tier, and fixes the family glitch so family members locked out of subsidies by unaffordable employer coverage can get them.

Requires providers enrolled in Medicare or Medicaid to also participate in the public plan, and bars providers who restrict or steer public-plan patients from federal health programs — protecting access to the plan's network.
Authorizes $10 billion per year for 2026-2028 to pool the costs of the most expensive patients nationwide, directly lowering premiums in the individual market.

Amends the Medicare drug pricing statute under the heading 'Authority to Negotiate Fair Prices for Medicare Prescription Drugs,' and sets the public plan's drug payments at rates negotiated by the HHS Secretary, potentially alongside Medicare's negotiated drug prices.
Puts $50 million into the Justice Department's antitrust division and $100 million into the FTC specifically to study and prosecute anticompetitive practices in health care markets.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government-backed competitor selling on the same exchanges. Hospitals and physician practices would be paid Medicare rates — well below what commercial insurers pay — and would have to join the plan to keep their Medicare and Medicaid enrollment, with an opt-out only in exceptional circumstances. Brand-name drug makers would face the plan paying Secretary-negotiated prices. Federal taxpayers would fund $2 billion in startup appropriations, $30 billion in reinsurance over three years, and a substantially larger and uncapped premium tax credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, hospitals, drug makers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The fiscal cost is large and partly open-ended: $2 billion in immediate startup appropriations, $30 billion authorized for reinsurance over 2026-2028, and removal of the 400%-of-poverty cap means premium subsidies would flow to high earners with no income ceiling, adding a permanent federal expense.

Doctors and hospitals would be forced into the plan to keep their Medicare and Medicaid enrollment, and could opt out only in 'exceptional circumstances' where participation threatens their ability to operate — a heavy mandate that could strain financially fragile providers, especially rural hospitals, even though rural areas could receive up to 50% higher Medicare rates.

The plan would pay providers at Medicare rates, which are substantially below what commercial insurers pay, so hospitals and medical practices would absorb significant revenue cuts that opponents argue could shrink provider networks.
The rollout is slow: most people would not have access until plan year 2029, so relief for high-premium markets would be years away even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real, targeted help — a public option aimed first at monopoly insurance markets, uncapped subsidies for families the current law strands, and money to fight health care consolidation — but at a genuine price: tens of billions in new federal spending, an uncapped subsidy entitlement, and mandatory below-commercial payment rates imposed on providers. The rural rate increase and reinsurance pool soften the blow to hospitals, and the premium savings for families in uncompetitive markets could be substantial. On balance the design is more carefully hedged than a pure public option, though its costs were never scored because it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2024 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the Medicare-X Choice Act on June 20, 2024, with eight original Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over health insurance legislation.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired in committee.
All 10 cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican ever signed on, and with Democrats holding only 48 of 100 Senate seats the bill had no path to passage without Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, hospital systems, and brand-name drug makers are better off because the bill never advanced — they avoid a Medicare-rate public competitor, a mandatory participation mandate, and negotiated drug prices. Families in one-insurer markets and households above the subsidy cliff gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 20, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the action record shows no committee action after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — all 10 cosponsors were Democrats out of 48 — with no Republican cosponsor and no vote ever taken to test the split.

industries.note: The bill puts a government-run plan on the same exchanges — starting in areas where insurers face little competition and reaching every rating area by 2029 — with free startup capital and Medicare-based provider rates. Insurers' interest in keeping premiums high where they face no competition runs directly against the public's interest in a cheaper alternative.

Providers would be required to join the plan to keep Medicare and Medicaid enrollment and would be paid at Medicare rates, which are well below commercial rates. Rural providers could see up to 50% higher rates and the $30 billion reinsurance pool would stabilize their markets, so the hit is uneven across the sector.

The public plan would pay for prescription drugs at rates the HHS Secretary negotiates, potentially in conjunction with Medicare's negotiated prices, and the bill amends the Medicare drug pricing statute under the heading 'Authority to Negotiate Fair Prices.' Lower negotiated drug prices would come out of manufacturer revenue.
The bill directs HHS to contract out the public plan's administrative functions the same way Medicare does, creating new federal contracting work for existing Medicare administrative contractors.
